name: Cervical Radiculopathy
summary: Cervical radiculopathy means a cervical nerve root is irritated or compressed, causing arm symptoms that follow that root's pattern. The most commonly affected roots are C6 and C7.
redFlags: Bilateral limb symptoms, gait change, clumsy hands, Hoffmann or Babinski
Progressive or severe motor loss (for example grade 3 or below, or worsening day to day)
Bladder or bowel change with limb signs
firstSteps: Initial approach: education and active exercise, for stable mild to moderate cases.
Justifying findings: root-pattern signs, no red flags, mild stable deficit.
Priority: education, then movement and strengthening.
aka: pinched nerve in neck arm pain from neck cervical disc nerve root

name: Cervical Myelopathy
summary: Cervical myelopathy means the spinal cord in the neck is under pressure or has been injured. The most common cause in adults is degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal (disc bulges, bony spurs, thickened ligaments).
redFlags: Rapidly worsening weakness, gait or hand function
Bladder or bowel change with new limb signs
Acute neck trauma plus neurological signs
firstSteps: Initial approach: recognise, document, refer. No neck loading.
Justifying findings: UMN signs, hand and gait change.
Priority: safe referral at the right urgency.
aka: spinal cord compression neck clumsy hands DCM degenerative cervical myelopathy

name: Cervicogenic Headache
summary: Cervicogenic headache is a headache that arises from a problem in the neck, usually the upper cervical joints (C0–C3) or related structures. Pain from these areas can be felt in the head because the upper cervical nerves and the trigeminal system share connections in the brainstem.
redFlags: Sudden, worst-ever headache
Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion or rash
Neck pain or headache with dizziness, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, facial numbness, balance loss
firstSteps: Initial approach: education plus manual therapy and exercise.
Justifying findings: one-sided neck-origin headache, neck triggers, reduced flexion-rotation, familiar response on palpation.
Priority: exercise and education, with manual therapy as an adjunct.
aka: headache from the neck neck headache occipital headache

name: Whiplash-Associated Disorders (WAD)
summary: Whiplash describes an acceleration-deceleration injury to the neck, most often from a rear-end or side-impact car crash. The resulting symptoms are called whiplash-associated disorders (WAD).
redFlags: Midline bony tenderness, high-risk mechanism, age 65 or over, limb paraesthesia after trauma
Bilateral limb symptoms, gait disturbance, bladder change
Dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks, nystagmus, numbness of the face
firstSteps: Initial approach: screen with the Canadian C-spine rule, then reassure and activate.
Priority: early movement and confidence.
Manual therapy: adjunct only.
aka: whiplash neck injury car accident neck WAD

name: Non-specific (Mechanical) Neck Pain
summary: Non-specific neck pain is neck pain, with or without referred shoulder or upper back pain, for which no specific serious or neurological cause is found. It is one of the most common musculoskeletal problems.
redFlags: Fever, night sweats, recent infection, IV drug use
Cancer history, unexplained weight loss, constant night pain
Bilateral hand clumsiness, gait change
firstSteps: Visit 1: screen flags, educate (good prognosis, stay active), start range exercises, consider manual therapy.
Weeks 2 to 6: strengthen deep flexors, scapular and upper back muscles; progress load.
Weeks 6 onward: endurance, work and sport demands, self-management plan for recurrences.
aka: neck pain stiff neck text neck cervical spondylosis cervical pain gardan dard

name: Cervical Artery Dysfunction and Upper Cervical Instability
summary: The internal carotid and vertebral arteries carry blood to the brain through the neck. A dissection is a tear in the inner wall of an artery that can lead to a clot and a stroke.
redFlags: New severe unusual neck pain or headache with any of the 5 Ds, 3 Ns or ataxia
Horner syndrome, visual loss, one-sided weakness
Positive Sharp-Purser or alar test, bilateral limb paraesthesia
firstSteps: Risk factors but no signs: choose low-force treatment (exercise, mid-range mobilisation); avoid manipulation; monitor; explain.
No concerns: proceed with the appropriate neck pathway, using informed consent.
aka: vertebral artery VBI cervical artery dissection upper cervical instability neck manipulation screening

name: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS)
summary: The thoracic outlet is the space between the collarbone and the first rib through which the brachial plexus, subclavian artery and subclavian vein pass to the arm. Compression can occur at three sites: between the scalene muscles, between the clavicle and first rib, and under the pectoralis minor.
redFlags: Sudden arm swelling and blue colour
Cold, white, painful fingers, absent pulse
Progressive hand weakness and wasting
firstSteps: Positional arm symptoms, normal neuro exam, positive provocation, supraclavicular tenderness: working diagnosis neurogenic TOS.
Start conservative care for at least several months before surgical opinion.
aka: TOS thoracic outlet arm numbness overhead brachial plexus

name: Rotator Cuff-related Shoulder Pain
summary: The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis) whose tendons surround the shoulder joint. They keep the ball centred in the socket and help lift and rotate the arm.
redFlags: Chest pain, sweating, breathlessness with left shoulder or arm pain
Fall or injury with deformity, inability to move the arm, or severe pain
Sudden inability to lift the arm after injury or lift, especially under 60 years
firstSteps: Initial approach: education and graded exercise.
Justifying findings: lateral shoulder pain, painful arc, resisted pain, full passive range, no flags.
Priority: tendon loading and function.
aka: rotator cuff related shoulder pain impingement subacromial pain painful arc shoulder pain overhead

name: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)
summary: Adhesive capsulitis, or frozen shoulder, is a condition in which the shoulder becomes painful and stiff, and passive range is clearly reduced in a typical pattern. The joint capsule is thought to become inflamed and thickened.
redFlags: Stiff shoulder after a seizure, electric shock or high-energy fall, with severely reduced external rotation
Hot swollen shoulder with fever
Constant severe night pain with weight loss, cancer history
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, pain control and symptom-guided movement.
Justifying findings: painful stiff shoulder, reduced passive range with external rotation worst, no trauma or red flags.
Priority: match treatment to phase.
aka: frozen shoulder stiff shoulder shoulder freezing capsulitis

name: Glenohumeral Instability
summary: The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body. A shallow socket (glenoid) holds a large ball (humeral head), so stability depends on the labrum, ligaments, capsule and the rotator cuff and scapular muscles.
redFlags: Visible deformity, cannot move the arm after injury
Numb or pale, cool, pulseless hand; severe swelling
Numbness over the lateral upper arm, weak deltoid
firstSteps: Initial approach: safe medical care for acute injury, then rehabilitation.
Justifying findings: apprehension, relocation, history, nerve status.
Priority: dynamic stability and confidence.
aka: dislocated shoulder shoulder dislocation shoulder subluxation Bankart instability

name: Acromioclavicular (AC) Joint Injury
summary: The acromioclavicular (AC) joint joins the outer end of the collarbone (clavicle) to the acromion, the bony tip of the shoulder blade. It is supported by the AC ligaments and the stronger coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments.
redFlags: Skin tenting or severely raised bone end
Visible clavicle deformity, bruising along bone, cannot lift arm
Hand numb, pale, cold, pulseless, or severe swelling
firstSteps: Initial approach: protection, pain control and early graded movement.
Justifying findings: local tenderness, mechanism, painful cross-body test, no fracture signs.
Priority: restore range, scapular control and strength.
aka: AC joint separated shoulder AC sprain

name: Glenohumeral Osteoarthritis
summary: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (GH OA) is a degenerative condition of the ball-and-socket shoulder joint in which the joint cartilage thins and the bone changes, with pain and stiffness. It is less common than knee or hip OA and is more often seen in older adults, after past shoulder injury or dislocation, after some surgeries, or with long-standing rotator cuff problems.
redFlags: Hot, swollen shoulder with fever
Sudden severe pain after minimal trauma in an older or steroid-treated patient
Rapid deterioration over weeks, severe night pain
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, activity modification and graded exercise.
Justifying findings: gradual pain, loss of passive external rotation, crepitus, X-ray changes, no flags.
Priority: function and pain control.
aka: shoulder arthritis shoulder OA

name: Biceps-related Shoulder Pain and Biceps Tendon Rupture
summary: The biceps brachii has two heads. The long head passes through the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder and attaches inside the joint to the top of the socket (the labrum).
redFlags: Chest pain, sweating, breathlessness
Sudden pop at the elbow with weak forearm supination and flexion, young or active person
Proximal rupture with severe weakness or in a high-demand worker or athlete
firstSteps: Initial approach: education and progressive tendon loading.
Justifying findings: front shoulder pain, groove tenderness, positive Speed or Yergason, no flags.
Priority: tendon capacity and function.
aka: biceps tendinitis biceps tendon pain front of shoulder biceps rupture Popeye

name: Proximal Humerus and Clavicle Fractures
summary: Proximal humerus fractures occur at the top of the upper arm bone, usually in older adults with osteoporosis after a fall onto an outstretched hand or directly onto the shoulder. Most are minimally displaced and treated without surgery in a sling, followed by early movement.
redFlags: Cold, pale hand, weak or absent pulse
New or worsening numbness or weakness
Increasing pain and deformity during rehabilitation
firstSteps: Phase 1 (about 0 to 3 weeks): protect, control pain, keep the hand, elbow and neck moving, early gentle shoulder movement as allowed.
Phase 2 (about 3 to 6 weeks): restore range.
Phase 3 (from about 6 to 12 weeks): strength, function, return to activity.
aka: broken shoulder humerus fracture collarbone fracture clavicle

name: Rotator Cuff Repair Rehabilitation
summary: A torn rotator cuff tendon is reattached to the humerus with anchors and sutures. Tendon-to-bone healing is slow, and re-tear is a known complication, more common in large tears, older patients and poor tissue quality.
redFlags: Fever, wound redness, discharge
Sudden pain and loss of active movement after an incident
Increasing stiffness in all directions, severe night pain
firstSteps: 1: Protection: About 0 to 6 weeks; Sling; elbow, wrist, hand, neck exercises; pendulum; passive or assisted range within limits; Active lifting, resisted exercise, lifting objects
2: Active range: About 6 to 12 weeks; Active-assisted to active elevation, rotation; scapular control; Heavy loading
aka: rotator cuff surgery cuff repair rehab

name: Lateral Elbow Tendinopathy (Tennis Elbow)
summary: Lateral elbow tendinopathy, commonly called tennis elbow, is a load-related tendon problem at the outer elbow where the wrist and finger extensor muscles attach to the lateral epicondyle, a bony point on the outside of the elbow. The extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon is most often involved.
redFlags: Fall or injury with swelling, inability to straighten or rotate the arm
Hot, red, swollen elbow with fever
Progressive weakness or wasting, numbness in the hand or fingers
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, load management and progressive loading.
Justifying findings: outer elbow pain, epicondyle tenderness, pain on resisted wrist extension, normal elbow range.
Priority: tendon capacity and grip function.
aka: tennis elbow lateral elbow tendinopathy lateral epicondylitis outer elbow pain

name: Medial Elbow Tendinopathy (Golfer's Elbow)
summary: Medial elbow tendinopathy is a load-related problem of the common flexor-pronator tendon at the medial epicondyle (inner elbow). It is less common than lateral elbow tendinopathy.
redFlags: Trauma with deformity or inability to move
Progressive hand weakness or wasting
Hot swollen elbow with fever
firstSteps: Medial pain on resisted flexion and pronation, local tenderness, normal range, no laxity: working diagnosis medial elbow tendinopathy.
Ulnar symptoms? Treat nerve sensitivity alongside.
aka: golfer's elbow medial elbow tendinopathy medial epicondylitis inner elbow pain

name: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Nerve at the Elbow)
summary: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel. Elbow flexion stretches the nerve and narrows the tunnel, increasing pressure.
redFlags: Progressive wasting or weakness
Wasting with fasciculations, no sensory loss
Bilateral hand symptoms, gait change
firstSteps: Ulnar sensory symptoms, positive elbow flexion test, no progressive motor loss: working diagnosis mild to moderate cubital tunnel syndrome. Start conservative care.
Weakness or wasting, or no improvement after about 3 months: refer for nerve conduction studies and surgical opinion.
aka: ulnar nerve elbow little finger tingling funny bone

name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS)
summary: The carpal tunnel is a passage at the front of the wrist formed by the carpal bones and the transverse carpal ligament. The median nerve and nine flexor tendons pass through it.
redFlags: Sudden severe symptoms after wrist trauma or fracture
Constant numbness with thenar wasting
Bilateral hand clumsiness with gait change
firstSteps: Mild to moderate (intermittent symptoms, no wasting): conservative care for about 6 to 12 weeks.
Severe (constant numbness, wasting) or failed conservative care: refer for nerve studies and surgical opinion.
aka: CTS median nerve tingling fingers numb hands at night

name: De Quervain Tenosynovitis
summary: De Quervain tenosynovitis is a painful condition of the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment at the thumb side of the wrist. The tendon sheath thickens, causing pain with thumb and wrist movement.
redFlags: Fall with snuffbox tenderness
Hot, red, swollen tendon sheath with fever
firstSteps: Radial styloid tenderness, positive Finkelstein or WHAT test, negative grind test: working diagnosis De Quervain tenosynovitis.
Start thumb spica splint, activity change and graded loading. If no improvement in 6 to 8 weeks, medical review for injection.
aka: mother's wrist thumb tendon pain texting thumb wrist thumb side pain

name: Distal Radius Fracture Rehabilitation
summary: The distal radius fracture is one of the most common fractures, especially in older women with osteoporosis after a fall on the outstretched hand. A Colles fracture has dorsal displacement of the fragment; a Smith fracture has palmar displacement.
redFlags: Rapid swelling, numbness, severe pain in cast
Disproportionate burning pain, colour and temperature change, sweating
Sudden inability to extend the thumb
firstSteps: During immobilisation: finger, elbow and shoulder movement.
After cast or early after volar plate: active range, then strengthening.
aka: wrist fracture Colles fracture broken wrist

name: Scaphoid Fracture
summary: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually in young adults after a fall on the outstretched hand. Its blood supply enters from the distal end, so fractures of the waist or proximal pole risk non-union and avascular necrosis (bone death) if missed.
redFlags: Fall plus snuffbox or tubercle tenderness, even with a normal X-ray
Wrist pain months after a "sprain"
Swelling and deformity
firstSteps: Immobilisation can be long (often 6 to 12 weeks or more depending on site). During immobilisation, keep the fingers, elbow and shoulder moving.
aka: scaphoid wrist fracture snuffbox

name: Trigger Finger and Common Finger Tendon Injuries
summary: Trigger finger: Thickened flexor tendon or A1 pulley; the tendon catches as the finger bends and straightens. Mallet finger: Extensor tendon torn or avulsed at the end joint; fingertip droops.
redFlags: Unable to flex fingertip after a pull injury
Penetrating injury with loss of flexion or numbness
Red, swollen finger, pain on passive extension, held flexed
firstSteps: Mallet finger: continuous extension splint for the DIP.
Trigger finger: splint and activity change; refer for injection if persistent.
aka: stenosing tenosynovitis finger locking finger catching mallet finger finger tendon injury

name: Mechanical Thoracic Spine Pain
summary: The thoracic spine has 12 vertebrae, each joined to a pair of ribs. This rib attachment makes the region stiffer than the neck or lower back.
redFlags: Chest or interscapular pain with sweating, nausea, breathlessness
Sudden tearing pain, BP difference between arms, collapse
Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, calf swelling
firstSteps: Screen; educate about mechanical nature and good prognosis.
Manual therapy and mobility exercise early.
Strengthening and posture variety; ergonomic adjustments.
aka: mid back pain upper back pain thoracic pain between shoulder blades

name: Rib-related Pain: Rib Dysfunction, Costochondritis and Rib Fracture
summary: Ribs attach to the spine at the back (costovertebral and costotransverse joints) and to the sternum at the front through cartilage (costochondral and sternocostal joints). Pain can arise at either end.
redFlags: Chest pain with sweating, breathlessness, arm or jaw radiation
Sudden breathlessness after trauma, reduced breath sounds
Multiple rib fractures, paradoxical chest movement
firstSteps: Trauma or fragility? Rule out fracture.
Localised reproducible pain, no systemic or exertional features: working diagnosis musculoskeletal chest wall pain (costochondritis or rib dysfunction).
aka: rib pain costochondritis rib fracture rib dysfunction chest wall pain

name: Thoracic Serious Pathology and Visceral Referred Pain
summary: Internal organs share nerve pathways with the thoracic spine segments. Pain from an organ can therefore be felt in the back or chest wall.
redFlags: Sudden tearing interscapular pain
Thoracic pain with leg weakness or bladder change
Cancer history with new thoracic pain
firstSteps: Neurological signs in the legs? Urgent or emergency referral.
All clear: proceed with the mechanical thoracic pathway (Vol 3 Ch 1).
aka: visceral referred pain thoracic red flags chest pain referred to back

name: Non-specific Low Back Pain
summary: Non-specific low back pain (NSLBP) means pain in the lower back, with or without leg pain above the knee, where no specific cause such as fracture, tumour, infection or nerve compression can be identified. Most back pain seen in clinics is in this group.
redFlags: Saddle numbness or tingling, new bladder or bowel dysfunction, new sexual dysfunction
Bilateral leg pain or weakness with progression
Major trauma, or minor trauma with older age, osteoporosis or long-term steroid use
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, reassurance and staying active.
Justifying findings: mechanical pattern, no flags, no nerve signs.
Priority: exercise and function over passive treatment.
aka: low back pain backache lumbago kamar dard nonspecific LBP mechanical back pain

name: Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica from a Nerve Root)
summary: Lumbar radiculopathy means a lumbar or sacral nerve root is irritated or compressed, causing leg pain and sometimes numbness or weakness in the area supplied by that root. The most common cause is disc herniation, followed by narrowing of the exit space from degeneration.
redFlags: Saddle numbness, new urinary retention or incontinence, bowel change, sexual dysfunction
Rapidly progressive or severe weakness (for example foot drop worsening within days)
Bilateral sciatica
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, staying active and symptom-guided exercise.
Justifying findings: below-knee pain, root signs, positive neural tension tests, no flags.
Priority: movement and function.
aka: sciatica slipped disc disc herniation prolapse sciatic nerve leg pain from back radiating leg pain

name: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES)
summary: The cauda equina (Latin for horse's tail) is the bundle of nerve roots that runs below the end of the spinal cord, in the lower lumbar canal. These roots supply the legs, the bladder, the bowel, the genital area and the saddle area (inner thighs, buttocks, perineum).
redFlags: Saddle numbness or altered sensation
New bladder or bowel dysfunction
New sexual dysfunction with back pain
firstSteps: Initial approach: recognise and refer the same day.
Justifying findings: saddle sensory change, bladder, bowel or sexual change, bilateral progressive signs.
Priority: speed and clear communication.
aka: CES saddle numbness bladder bowel back emergency

name: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
summary: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) means narrowing of the space for the nerves in the lumbar spine. The narrowing can be in the central canal, the lateral recess or the exit foramen.
redFlags: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction
Rapidly worsening weakness or falls
Cold, painful, pale or pulseless leg
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, flexion-tolerant exercise, supported walking.
Justifying findings: walking-related bilateral symptoms eased by sitting or flexion, normal pulses.
Priority: walking tolerance, fitness and function.
aka: spinal stenosis neurogenic claudication leg pain walking narrowing

name: Spondylolysis and Spondylolisthesis
summary: Spondylolysis is a defect or stress injury (a crack or break) in the pars interarticularis, the small bridge of bone joining the upper and lower facet joints of a lumbar vertebra. It is a common cause of back pain in young athletes who repeatedly extend and rotate the spine, for example in gymnastics, cricket fast bowling, diving and weightlifting.
redFlags: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction
Progressive weakness or foot drop
Child or adolescent with severe pain, visible deformity or gait change
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, load management and active trunk and hip rehabilitation.
Justifying findings: extension-related pain, suggestive tests, no nerve loss or flags.
Priority: protect healing in young athletes; build trunk control in adults.
aka: spondylolysis spondylolisthesis pars fracture slipped vertebra

name: Pelvic Girdle Pain and Sacroiliac-region Pain
summary: Pelvic girdle pain (PGP) is pain felt between the back of the pelvis (the area between the iliac crest and the gluteal fold, near the sacroiliac joint) and sometimes at the front, over the pubic symphysis. It may spread to the buttock or the back of the thigh.
redFlags: Vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, leaking fluid, regular contractions in pregnancy
Severe headache with visual disturbance, sudden swelling, upper abdominal pain in pregnancy
Calf swelling, warmth, pain or sudden breathlessness
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, activity advice, a belt trial and a graded exercise program.
Justifying findings: posterior pelvic pain, positive ASLR or provocation cluster, no red flags.
Priority: improving function and confidence.
aka: sacroiliac joint SIJ pain pelvic pain pregnancy pelvic girdle pain PGP

name: Hip Osteoarthritis
summary: Hip osteoarthritis (hip OA) is a long-term condition of the hip ball-and-socket joint in which the cartilage thins and the bone and surrounding tissues change. It causes pain, stiffness and loss of function, and it is a common reason for walking difficulty in older adults.
redFlags: After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened and externally rotated leg, severe groin pain
Hot swollen hip with fever, severe pain on any movement
Adolescent with hip, thigh or knee pain and a limp
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, exercise and weight management when relevant.
Justifying findings: age, groin pain, reduced internal rotation, no flags.
Priority: strength, fitness and function.
aka: hip arthritis hip OA hip wear

name: Gluteal Tendinopathy and Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome
summary: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) means pain over the outer (lateral) hip, centred on the greater trochanter, the bony point on the side of the hip. It is a descriptive label.
redFlags: Pain with impact, a runner or someone with low bone density or low energy intake
After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened leg, severe pain
Hot swollen hip or lateral thigh with fever
firstSteps: Initial approach: education to reduce tendon compression, load management and progressive strengthening.
Justifying findings: outer hip pain, trochanter tenderness, single-leg stance pain, full hip range, no flags.
Priority: build tendon and abductor capacity while reducing compression.
aka: GTPS trochanteric bursitis side of hip pain lateral hip pain gluteal tendon

name: Hamstring Injury
summary: The hamstrings are three muscles at the back of the thigh (biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus). They extend the hip and bend the knee, and they work hard to slow the lower leg in the late swing phase of running.
redFlags: Sudden severe pain, large bruise, palpable gap, unable to walk, often after a stretch or slide
Severe tense swelling and escalating pain
Numbness, weakness below the knee, foot drop
firstSteps: Initial approach: exclude avulsion and nerve problems, then early graded loading.
Justifying findings: mechanism, local tenderness, pain on resisted flexion, no gap.
Priority: strength, lengthened capacity and running readiness.
aka: hamstring injury pulled hamstring hamstring tear back of thigh pain sprinter

name: Femoroacetabular Impingement Syndrome and Labral Presentations
summary: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint. The ball is the femoral head and the socket is the acetabulum.
redFlags: Adolescent with a limp and limited or painful hip rotation
Pain with impact, runner or low bone density
After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened externally rotated leg
firstSteps: Initial approach: screen flags, then education, activity modification and exercise therapy.
Justifying findings: motion-related groin pain, positive FADIR, reduced flexion and internal rotation, imaging shape.
Priority: build hip and trunk strength and control, avoid provoking positions early.
aka: FAI hip impingement cam pincer labral tear groin pain hip

name: Hip Fracture
summary: Hip fracture means a fracture of the proximal femur: intracapsular (femoral neck) or extracapsular (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric). Most occur in older adults after a fall from standing height.
redFlags: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, tachycardia, low SpO2
Systolic BP drop with dizziness or loss of consciousness
Leg shortening and rotation after movement
firstSteps: Pre-operative: chest care, positioning, explain the plan.
Day 0 to 1: mobilise out of bed.
Ward: daily walking, transfers, ADL with occupational therapy.
aka: neck of femur fracture broken hip fall older adult

name: Groin Pain in Athletes (Adductor-related, Inguinal-related and Pubic-related)
summary: Groin pain is common in sports with kicking, sprinting and change of direction (football, cricket fielding, hockey). The Doha agreement classified athletic groin pain into clinical entities:
redFlags: Groin pain with pain on hopping in an endurance athlete or female athlete with low energy availability
Testicular pain and swelling, sudden
Fever, severe pain on any hip movement
firstSteps: Manual therapy has a minor role (soft-tissue work for comfort). Exercise is the core:
aka: groin strain adductor strain groin pain footballer inguinal pubic

name: Paediatric Hip and Knee Conditions: DDH, Perthes Disease, SCFE and Osgood-Schlatter
summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH): Birth to infancy. Transient synovitis: 3 to 10 years.
redFlags: Fever, unwell, refusing to bear weight, severe pain on any hip movement
Adolescent with hip, thigh or knee pain and obligatory external rotation; unable to bear weight
Night pain, weight loss, bruising, pallor
firstSteps: Young child, gradual limp, reduced IR? Perthes: orthopaedic referral.
Active adolescent with tuberosity pain, normal hip? Osgood-Schlatter: load management.
aka: DDH hip dysplasia Perthes SCFE slipped upper femoral epiphysis Osgood-Schlatter child limp

name: Knee Osteoarthritis
summary: Knee osteoarthritis (knee OA) is a long-term joint condition in which the whole knee is affected: cartilage, bone, the joint lining, ligaments and the muscles around it. It is one of the most common causes of pain and walking difficulty in adults.
redFlags: Hot, red, swollen knee with fever or unable to move the joint
Sudden hot swollen painful joint, no fever
Injury with inability to take weight, bony tenderness, or inability to bend to 90 degrees, age 55 or older
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, exercise and weight management when relevant.
Justifying findings: age, activity-related pain, short stiffness, crepitus, no flags.
Priority: build strength, fitness and confidence.
aka: knee arthritis knee OA ghutno ka dard

name: Patellofemoral Pain
summary: Patellofemoral pain (PFP) is pain at the front of the knee, around or behind the kneecap (patella), that is made worse by loading the joint between the kneecap and the thigh bone, for example when squatting, climbing stairs, running or sitting for a long time. It is common in active young adults, especially women and runners, and in adolescents.
redFlags: Adolescent with knee pain, limp and limited or painful hip rotation
Hot, red, swollen knee with fever
Fall or injury with immediate swelling, inability to bear weight or a visible deformity
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, load management and exercise therapy.
Justifying findings: anterior knee pain, typical triggers, positive squat or step-down, no flags.
Priority: build knee and hip strength and load tolerance.
aka: PFPS kneecap pain runner's knee anterior knee pain

name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injury
summary: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is a strong band inside the knee that stops the shin bone (tibia) from sliding too far forward under the thigh bone (femur) and helps control twisting. An ACL injury is usually a sprain or a tear.
redFlags: Gross instability in several directions, severe swelling, history of a high-energy injury
Cold, pale or pulseless foot
Foot drop or numbness over the outer lower leg and top of foot
firstSteps: Initial approach: safety screen, swelling control, extension and quadriceps activation.
Justifying findings: mechanism, swelling, positive Lachman or pivot shift.
Priority: a clear decision about rehabilitation first or surgery, with a criteria-based plan.
aka: ACL tear anterior cruciate ligament cruciate knee giving way

name: Meniscal Injury
summary: The menisci are two C-shaped pads of fibrocartilage (medial and lateral) between the thigh bone and the shin bone. They share load, add stability and help nourish the joint.
redFlags: Locked knee: true block to full extension
Hot red swollen knee with fever
Gross instability, severe swelling, history of high-energy injury
firstSteps: Initial approach: screen for a locked knee, then education and exercise therapy.
Justifying findings: joint-line tenderness, twisting history, positive tests, no true block.
Priority: restore range, strength and function.
aka: meniscus tear cartilage tear knee locking torn cartilage

name: Patellar Tendinopathy
summary: The patellar tendon connects the lower edge (inferior pole) of the kneecap to the shin bone (tibial tuberosity). It stores and releases energy in jumping, landing and changes of direction.
redFlags: Sudden pop and inability to straighten the knee against gravity, palpable gap, high-riding patella
Recent steroid injection or fluoroquinolone use with new severe pain
Hot red swollen knee with fever
firstSteps: Initial approach: exclude rupture, then education, load management and progressive loading.
Justifying findings: localised lower pole pain, decline squat positive, load-related pattern.
Priority: tendon capacity and sport readiness.
aka: jumper's knee patellar tendinitis

name: Knee Collateral and Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
summary: Ligament sprains are graded: grade I (stretch, no laxity), grade II (partial tear, some laxity with a firm end point), grade III (complete tear, laxity without a firm end point). Most isolated MCL injuries heal well with conservative management.
redFlags: Laxity of several ligaments, high-energy trauma
Foot drop after lateral injury
Ottawa rule positive
firstSteps: Typical return to sport: grade I MCL a few weeks; grade II longer; grade III and PCL longer still. Base return on criteria, not time alone.
aka: MCL LCL PCL collateral ligament knee sprain posterior cruciate

name: ACL Reconstruction Rehabilitation
summary: ACL reconstruction replaces the torn ligament with a graft (commonly hamstring tendons, patellar tendon, or quadriceps tendon). The graft goes through a period of weakening and remodelling ("ligamentisation") over many months, so rehabilitation and return to sport must respect biology and meet functional criteria.
redFlags: Calf pain and swelling
Fever, red hot wound, increasing swelling
Loss of extension that does not improve (block)
firstSteps: 1: Early (about 0 to 2 weeks): Swelling control, full extension, quadriceps activation (quads sets, SLR), walking with crutches as needed; Full extension, SLR without lag, minimal effusion, normal gait
2: Strength (about 2 to 12 weeks): Closed and open chain strengthening, balance, cycling; Effusion trace or less, full range, good single-leg control
aka: ACL surgery ACL reconstruction rehab after ACL operation graft

name: Total Knee and Total Hip Arthroplasty Rehabilitation
summary: Joint replacement replaces damaged joint surfaces with artificial components for advanced osteoarthritis or other joint destruction. Modern enhanced recovery pathways mobilise patients on the day of surgery or the next day, with short hospital stays.
redFlags: Sudden hip pain, leg shortened and rotated after a movement (THA)
Calf pain and swelling, sudden breathlessness
Wound discharge, fever, increasing pain
firstSteps: Discharge when safe with home exercise.
Outpatient: range, strength, function, return to activities.
aka: TKR TKA THR THA knee replacement hip replacement

name: Lateral Ankle Sprain
summary: The outer (lateral) ankle is held by three main ligaments: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL). A lateral ankle sprain is a stretch or tear of these ligaments, most often the ATFL, when the foot turns inward under the body (inversion with plantar flexion), for example when landing or stepping on uneven ground.
redFlags: Ottawa rule positive, deformity, or severe pain
Pale, cold or pulseless foot, or severe swelling with intense pain
Numbness, foot drop
firstSteps: Initial approach: apply the Ottawa rules, protect and begin early graded loading.
Justifying findings: mechanism, outer ankle swelling, positive drawer or tilt, no fracture signs.
Priority: restore range, strength and balance.
aka: ankle sprain twisted ankle rolled ankle

name: Plantar Heel Pain (Plantar Fasciopathy)
summary: The plantar fascia is a strong band of tissue under the foot that runs from the heel bone (calcaneus) to the base of the toes and supports the arch. Plantar heel pain is pain under the heel, most often at the inner (medial) edge of the heel bone where the fascia attaches.
redFlags: Sudden tearing pain with a pop and swelling or bruising
Squeeze test positive or pain with impact in a runner or after a rise in training
Hot, red, swollen heel with fever
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, load management, strengthening and stretching, supportive footwear.
Justifying findings: first-step pain, medial heel tenderness, positive windlass test, negative squeeze test.
Priority: build load tolerance of the fascia and calf.
aka: plantar fasciitis plantar fasciopathy heel pain heel spur

name: Achilles Tendinopathy
summary: The Achilles tendon joins the calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) to the heel bone (calcaneus). It handles very high loads in walking, running and jumping.
redFlags: Sudden pop, inability to rise on the toes, positive Thompson test, palpable gap
Pain after recent fluoroquinolone antibiotic or steroid use
Hot red swollen heel with fever
firstSteps: Initial approach: exclude rupture, then education, load management and progressive loading.
Justifying findings: localised tendon pain and thickening, reduced heel raise capacity, no rupture signs.
Priority: build tendon and calf capacity.
aka: achilles tendinitis achilles pain back of heel

name: Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome and Bone Stress Injuries
summary: Medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS, "shin splints") is exercise-related pain along the inner border of the tibia over at least 5 cm, common in runners and military recruits. Bone stress injuries range from bone stress reaction to complete stress fracture, caused by repeated loading faster than bone can adapt.
redFlags: Focal tibial pain worsening with walking, night pain
Anterior tibial "dreaded black line" on X-ray, high-risk site
Groin pain with hopping in a runner
firstSteps: Diffuse medial tibial tenderness, no focal signs: working diagnosis MTSS.
Screen energy availability and bone health in all bone stress injuries.
aka: shin splints MTSS medial tibial stress syndrome stress fracture bone stress injury

name: Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident)
summary: A stroke is a sudden loss of brain function caused by interrupted blood supply: ischaemic (a blocked artery, most strokes) or haemorrhagic (bleeding). Brain cells in the affected area die or stop working, causing weakness, sensory loss, speech, vision, swallowing and cognitive problems depending on the area.
redFlags: New face, arm or speech change, sudden vision loss or imbalance
BP above the medically agreed limit, severe headache
Calf swelling, pain
firstSteps: Acute (days): stability, positioning, swallowing awareness, early graded mobilisation, chest care, prevention of complications.
Subacute (weeks to months): intensive task-specific practice; most rapid recovery occurs in the first months.
Chronic (after about 6 months): continued gains possible with practice; fitness, community walking, secondary prevention (exercise, BP control).
aka: stroke CVA paralysis hemiplegia falij

name: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) and Concussion
summary: TBI is brain damage from an external force: falls, road traffic accidents, assaults, sports. Severity is often classified by the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS): mild 13 to 15, moderate 9 to 12, severe 3 to 8.
redFlags: Drop in GCS, new confusion, unequal pupils
Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure after head injury
Neck pain with limb symptoms after head injury
firstSteps: Severe TBI: positioning and splinting to prevent contracture; tilt table and early standing when medically cleared; task-specific training; balance and gait; aerobic fitness; high-level mobility (running, jumping) for young patients returning to sport or work.
aka: TBI head injury concussion

name: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
summary: SCI damages the spinal cord, interrupting movement, sensation and autonomic control below the level of injury. Causes include trauma (road accidents, falls, gunshot) and non-traumatic causes (tumour, infection, disc, vascular).
redFlags: Sudden pounding headache, high BP, flushing and sweating above the injury, slow heart rate (injury at T6 or above)
Dizziness, fainting on sitting up
Leg swelling
firstSteps: Set goals based on level and AIS grade.
Train functional skills: rolling, transfers, wheelchair skills; walking practice for motor incomplete injuries.
aka: SCI paraplegia tetraplegia quadriplegia

name: Parkinson's Disease
summary: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease caused by loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra. Dopamine helps the basal ganglia produce smooth, well-scaled, automatic movement.
redFlags: Rapid deterioration over days
Sudden severe rigidity, fever, confusion after stopping medication
Fainting on standing
firstSteps: Middle stage (H&Y 2 to 4): add falls prevention, cueing strategies for freezing, transfers, dual-task training.
Late stage (H&Y 5): maintain transfers, prevent complications, train carers, positioning.
aka: Parkinson's tremor freezing of gait

name: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
summary: MS is an immune-mediated disease in which the protective myelin around nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord is damaged, slowing or blocking nerve signals. It is most often diagnosed in young adults, more often in women.
redFlags: New or worsening symptoms lasting more than 24 hours without fever
Worsening with fever or urinary symptoms
Sudden vision loss with eye pain
firstSteps: Stable: exercise program (aerobic, resistance, balance), fatigue management.
Progressive with high disability: maintain mobility, transfers, prevent contracture, equipment, carer training.
aka: MS demyelination fatigue

name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome and Peripheral Neuropathy
summary: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune attack on peripheral nerves, often after an infection. It causes rapidly progressive, usually symmetrical weakness starting in the legs and ascending, with reduced or absent reflexes.
redFlags: Rapidly ascending weakness, reduced reflexes
Falling vital capacity, weak cough, swallowing difficulty in GBS
Large swings in heart rate and BP in GBS
firstSteps: Daily foot checks, proper footwear, avoid barefoot walking.
Use vision and handrails at night; good lighting.
aka: GBS peripheral neuropathy diabetic neuropathy numb feet ascending weakness

name: Vestibular Disorders: BPPV and Vestibular Hypofunction
summary: The vestibular system in the inner ear senses head movement and gravity. It keeps the eyes stable during head movement (vestibulo-ocular reflex, VOR) and helps balance.
redFlags: Vertigo with double vision, dysarthria, dysphagia, numbness, weakness, unable to stand or walk
New severe headache or neck pain with vertigo
Sudden hearing loss
firstSteps: Post-manoeuvre restrictions are generally not necessary.
aka: BPPV vertigo dizziness vestibular hypofunction chakkar

name: Cerebral Palsy (CP)
summary: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance in the developing brain (before, during or soon after birth). The brain lesion does not get worse, but musculoskeletal problems (contractures, hip displacement, bone deformity) can progress as the child grows.
redFlags: Loss of previously gained skills (regression)
New hip pain, reduced abduction, asymmetry
Pain or swelling after minor trauma in a non-walking child
firstSteps: Choose interventions with evidence for those goals; review every few months.
Monitor hips and contractures as the child grows.
aka: CP child spasticity GMFCS

name: Developmental Motor Delay and Early Screening
summary: Motor delay means a child achieves motor milestones later than expected. It may be isolated, part of global developmental delay, or a sign of a specific condition (CP, neuromuscular disease, genetic syndromes).
redFlags: Loss of skills
Waddling gait, difficulty rising from the floor using hands on legs (Gowers sign), large calves in a boy
Marked hypotonia with weakness, poor feeding, weak cry
firstSteps: Early intervention: parent-coached, play-based motor practice in daily routines.
DCD: task-oriented training (for example CO-OP or neuromotor task training).
aka: late walking milestones delay baby development

name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
summary: COPD is a common, preventable lung disease with persistent airflow limitation and respiratory symptoms, usually caused by smoking, biomass fuel smoke or occupational exposure. It includes emphysema (destruction of alveoli and loss of elastic recoil) and chronic bronchitis (chronic productive cough).
redFlags: Acute severe breathlessness, unable to speak, confusion, drowsiness
Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness
Coughing blood
firstSteps: Initial approach: pulmonary rehabilitation with education.
Priority: exercise capacity, breathlessness management, self-management.
Techniques: breathing control, pursed-lip breathing, positions of ease, ACBT if sputum.
aka: COPD chronic bronchitis emphysema pulmonary rehabilitation breathlessness

name: Asthma
summary: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable, reversible airflow obstruction. Triggers (allergens, cold air, exercise, infections, smoke) cause bronchoconstriction, mucosal swelling and mucus.
redFlags: Unable to complete sentences, RR above about 25, HR above about 110, PEF 33 to 50% of best
Silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, PEF below 33%
Increasing reliever need over days
firstSteps: Well controlled? Exercise training, breathing retraining if dysfunctional breathing, inhaler and action plan education.
Exercise-induced symptoms? Warm-up strategy, pre-exercise reliever as prescribed, medical review if frequent.
aka: asthma wheeze breathing

name: Pneumonia, Sputum Retention and Airway Clearance
summary: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue: alveoli fill with inflammatory fluid (consolidation). Consolidation is not sputum in the airways, so airway clearance techniques do not remove it.
redFlags: Rising oxygen requirement, RR above about 30, confusion, falling BP
Haemoptysis (frank blood)
Sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness
firstSteps: Volume loss? Positioning, deep breathing, incentive spirometry, mobilisation.
Neither? Mobilisation and positioning; no routine chest clearance.
aka: pneumonia sputum retention chest physiotherapy airway clearance

name: Postoperative Respiratory Care (Abdominal and Thoracic Surgery)
summary: After major surgery, especially upper abdominal and thoracic surgery, anaesthesia, pain, opioids, immobility and reduced diaphragm function lower lung volumes. This can cause atelectasis, sputum retention, and postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) such as pneumonia.
redFlags: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, tachycardia
Rising RR, fever, new crackles or bronchial breathing
Low BP, high HR, increased drain output or wound bleeding
firstSteps: Chest drains: keep the drainage bottle below chest level, never lift above the patient, do not clamp unless instructed, watch for swinging and bubbling as instructed.
aka: after abdominal surgery after thoracic surgery chest physio post-op

name: Cardiac Rehabilitation (Coronary Artery Disease, Post-MI, PCI and CABG)
summary: Coronary artery disease (CAD) narrows the arteries supplying the heart muscle. A partial or temporary mismatch causes angina; a blocked artery causes myocardial infarction (MI).
redFlags: Chest pain at rest or not relieved by rest and GTN within minutes
New palpitations with dizziness or collapse
BP falling during exercise
firstSteps: Traditional precautions restrict lifting and pushing for about 6 to 8 weeks. Many centres now use more individual, movement-based approaches ("Keep Your Move in the Tube": keep upper arm movements close to the body during loaded tasks).
aka: cardiac rehab heart attack MI PCI stent CABG bypass

name: Heart Failure
summary: Heart failure is a syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs at normal filling pressures. Types: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), typically ejection fraction 40% or less, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).
redFlags: Breathless at rest, pink frothy sputum, cannot lie flat
Rapid weight gain, increasing oedema
New arrhythmia, ICD shock
firstSteps: Monitor HR, BP, SpO2, RPE, symptoms. Longer warm-up and cool-down.
aka: heart failure HF breathless swelling legs

name: Falls and Frailty in Older Adults
summary: A fall is an unexpected event in which a person comes to rest on the ground or a lower level. Falls in older adults lead to fractures, head injury, fear of falling, loss of independence and admission to care.
redFlags: Fall with blackout, palpitations, chest pain
Head injury on anticoagulants
Hip pain and inability to bear weight after a fall
firstSteps: Exercise that challenges balance, done regularly and for long enough, reduces falls. A widely used program is the Otago Exercise Programme.
aka: falls older adults frailty balance elderly

name: Osteoporosis
summary: Osteoporosis is a disease of low bone mass and deteriorated bone structure, leading to fragile bones and fractures from minimal trauma (fragility fractures), most commonly at the spine, hip and wrist. It is diagnosed by a DXA bone density scan (T-score of −2.5 or lower) or by a fragility fracture.
redFlags: Sudden severe back pain after minor activity
Hip pain after a fall, unable to weight-bear
Fracture with weight loss, night pain
firstSteps: Safe movement advice: avoid repeated, loaded, end-range spinal flexion combined with rotation (for example toe touches, sit-ups with twisting, lifting heavy objects with a rounded back) in people with high fracture risk or previous vertebral fractures. Teach hip hinge and neutral spine.
aka: weak bones fragility fracture bone density
